content.title: “I want nothing to do with hospitals anymore”: challenges, met and unmet needs of people experiencing homelessness with acquired brain injury
content.text: ABSTRACTPurpose People experiencing homelessness have a high prevalence of mental and physical health problems, including acquired brain injury (ABI), which leads to complex health and social needs. The literature highlights the challenging and often stigmatizing experiences people in situations of homelessness have within the various services involved in their care. This study aimed to identify the challenges, as well as the met and unmet needs, of people experiencing homelessness and ABI in their daily lives and across the services involved in their trajectories, both in community and institutional settings.Materials and methods A qualitative study involving 26 semi-structured interviews with people with a history of both homelessness and ABI was conducted. Data were analyzed using Paillé and Mucchielli’s method of thematic analysis.Results Participants reported 1) intersecting health and social challenges and needs related to ABI and comorbid conditions influence residential pathways, recovery, and service use; 2) fragmented and often inadequate service responses to complex and intersecting needs and challenges and 3) nonuse of health care services.Conclusion This study highlights the complex and diverse needs of people experiencing homelessness with an ABI, and emphasizes the urgent need for a coordinated, integrated approach to improve their experiences with services.IntroductionThis study is the second in a two-part series examining the life trajectories and turning points toward homelessness of people who have experienced homelessness and sustained an acquired brain injury (ABI), as well as the challenges they face and the areas where their needs are met or unmet in daily life and across the services involved in their care. The companion article focused on life trajectories and key moments in the lives of these individuals (Citation1), while this article reports on their experiences and challenges within the different services involved in their care trajectories, highlighting the needs that emerge from these accounts. We recommend that readers start with this first article to gain a better understanding of the data presented in this second paper.Several studies have shown that people experiencing homelessness have higher morbidity and mortality rates than the general population (Citation2–6). ABI, for example, is significantly more prevalent among people experiencing homelessness than in the general population (Citation7–11). The majority of studies examining the prevalence of ABI in people experiencing homelessness have focused on traumatic brain injury, although some data also confirm a high prevalence of non-traumatic ABI, such as ABI secondary to alcohol and other substance use and hypoxia (Citation10,Citation12–15). However, people experiencing homelessness have many other mental and physical health needs (Citation2,Citation16). Several studies and systematic reviews have shown a higher prevalence of psychiatric disorders in this population (Citation17–21) including substance use disorders, personality disorders, mood disorders, or psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia (Citation17–21). People experiencing homelessness also live with a range of physical health needs and are at higher risk for infectious diseases, certain chronic diseases, cardiovascular disease, chronic pain, as well as various and repeated injuries (Citation22–26). In addition, several studies have shown a high co-occurrence of both mental and physical health problems among people experiencing homelessness (Citation16,Citation27,Citation28). Homeless individuals therefore have complex, heterogeneous profiles from a health and social perspective (Citation16,Citation27,Citation28). Despite, or because of, their complex and extensive needs, people experiencing homelessness often report negative experiences within service systems, shaped by structural, organizational and relational factors that limit access to, and the quality of, care (Citation26,Citation29–34).Experiences in services and unmet needsPrevious studies have documented many difficult experiences in services and barriers to care for people experiencing homelessness in health and social service systems (Citation35–39). In this article, ‘care’ refers to a broad, integrated set of services delivered in community and institutional settings. These services include healthcare and social services, housing support, judicial services, and legal aid, among others. This reflects the integrated care model described by Kodner and Spreeuwenberg, which emphasizes coordinating person-centered services across the health, social, and community sectors to address complex, overlapping needs (Citation40). Omerov and colleagues conducted an integrative systematic review and identified three main categories of barriers to care: interpersonal dimensions of access to care, structural and organizational aspects of care that limit the ability of services to meet the needs of people experiencing homelessness, and unmet basic human needs that take precedence over seeking care (Citation37). Interpersonal dimensions limiting access to care include perceptions of judgment, stigmatization, lack of empathy and healthcare professionals’ failure to listen. These issues have been highlighted in several studies examining the experiences of people in situations of homelessness in healthcare services (Citation36,Citation37,Citation41–46). Structural and organizational aspects such as bureaucracy and rigid service hours are often identified as significant barriers to care (Citation37). Several studies have also highlighted the lack of a holistic approach to caring for people experiencing homelessness and the inability of health systems to address their physical and mental health needs in an integrated way. This contributes to fragmented and often challenging experiences of services (Citation42,Citation43,Citation47). Finally, unmet basic human needs, such as finding shelter or food, often take precedence over health concerns for this population. A lack of knowledge about available services and the possible consequences of certain health conditions that remain untreated have also been identified as important barriers to care (Citation37,Citation42,Citation48).ABI-specific services for people experiencing homelessnessWhile the vast majority of individuals experiencing homelessness face these interpersonal, structural and organizational barriers, as well as the challenges arising from unmet basic human needs, those who have sustained an ABI face additional, often overlooked challenges in accessing appropriate care (Citation49,Citation50). A few studies have examined the perceptions and experiences of community workers and health care professionals working in non-ABI specific services and organizations with regard to supporting people experiencing homelessness or housing instability who have sustained an ABI (Citation51–55). Campbell and colleagues assessed the perceived competence and interventions of emergency shelter workers for female victims of intimate partner violence who had sustained an ABI and showed that despite high levels of knowledge, workers felt inadequately trained to perform ABI screening, adjust their interventions to consider the sequelae of ABI, and refer patients to appropriate specialized ABI health services (Citation51). A review of rehabilitation services for homeless people with ABI by Chan and colleagues highlighted the lack of structured rehabilitation interventions tailored to the specific needs of this population and reported that current ABI rehabilitation services are often inaccessible or poorly suited to their needs and realities (Citation49). A recent study conducted in Canada identified several issues related to the care, or lack thereof, for people experiencing homelessness who have sustained an ABI (Citation50). Multiple barriers were identified, such as a mismatch between care structures and the realities experienced by people experiencing homelessness, a heavy reliance on homeless community organizations that are already overburdened and do not always have the necessary expertise to provide support to people who have sustained an ABI, and the need to rethink the organization of care by promoting intersectoral collaboration and offering more flexible and adapted services (Citation50). However, this latter study solely focused on the perspectives of those who work with homeless individuals who have sustained an ABI, i.e. health professionals, community workers and managers in these two settings, and not on the perspectives of the people experiencing homelessness themselves. Moreover, beyond the general issues of access to care documented in the literature, there is little data on the specific service experiences and service-related needs of people experiencing homelessness who have sustained an ABI. This limits the development of appropriate and responsive service approaches for people experiencing homelessness with ABI, as understanding their lived experiences and perceived intersecting service needs is essential to developing programs that meet these needs.Context of the present studyThis study is part of a broader collaborative knowledge synthesis project conducted in the province of Quebec, Canada (Citation56). For more information on the context of the study, please refer to the companion article (Citation1).The objectives of this study were to 1) identify the challenges, as well as the met and unmet needs, of people experiencing homelessness and ABI in their daily lives and across the services involved in their trajectories, including – but not limited to – health and social services, housing support, correctional and judicial services, delivered in both community and institutional settings and 2) understand the key moments and turning points toward homelessness for these individuals. This article focuses on the first objective: identifying the challenges, as well as the met and unmet needs of people experiencing homelessness and ABI in their daily lives and in services. The second objective – understanding turning points toward homelessness – is detailed in the companion article (Citation1).MethodsA descriptive qualitative design was used to conduct this study (Citation57). The companion article (Citation1) provides a detailed description of the participants, data collection and ethical considerations. Below, we present a concise summary with emphasis on the elements specific to this paper.ParticipantsCommunity organizations working in the field of homelessness and housing in two large Canadian cities contributed to participant recruitment. The research project was presented to the community workers from the partner organizations, who identified potential participants for the study from their respective caseloads and connected them with the research team. Potential participants were identified by community workers based on their knowledge of the participants’ life histories (e.g. involvement in numerous fights resulting in hits to the head) or ABI status, when available. The research team contacted all individuals who expressed an initial interest in participating, and none of them withdrew from the project after doing so. To participate, participants had to 1) be 18 years of age or older, 2) be homeless or have been homeless in the past five years as defined by European Typology of Homelessness and Housing Exclusion (ETHOS) (Citation58) and 3) have at least one diagnosed or suspected ABI. Participants who were unable to participate in a 60–90 minute interview in English or French were excluded. The recruitment process continued until data saturation was achieved (Citation59).Data collectionSemi-structured individual interviews were conducted by two occupational therapists and graduate students in rehabilitation sciences [WJ and RD], with relevant clinical and research experience in the field of homelessness and ABI. The interviews were held at times and locations chosen by the participants. Nineteen participants chose to conduct their interviews in private spaces within their community organizations. Five opted to conduct their interviews at home. One participant chose a research center affiliated with the study investigators, and one opted to conduct their interview in a park. Each participant received cash compensation for their time. After obtaining informed written consent, the interviewers administered a sociodemographic questionnaire and the Ohio State University TBI Identification Method (OSU-TBI-ID) (Citation60), to which an additional question from the Brief ABI Screen was added to account for non-traumatic ABIs. This questionnaire was used to describe all ABIs sustained in the participants’ lives. The questionnaire was translated into French using the back-translation method for French-speaking participants (Citation61). Individual interviews were then conducted using the life history mapping method, a biographical approach designed to visually chart participants’ life trajectories and capture the complexity of their life courses (Citation62,Citation63). Emphasis was placed on ABI related needs that influenced residential pathways and service use. Probing questions were used to explore participant’s service use throughout their life trajectories. This may have included questions such as, ‘Can you tell me about the people who had a positive or negative influence during that period?,’ ‘Can you tell me about the help or services you received after this incident?,’ and ‘Can you tell me if there were other supports you would have liked during that period?’ The full interview guide is provided in Appendix A. If participants did not spontaneously mention the ABI or services received when discussing their life trajectories, the interviewer asked service-related questions based on the results of the OSU-TBI-ID questionnaire. Overall, the data collection process averaged 75 minutes per participant.Data analysisAll interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The transcripts were then subjected to thematic analysis using Paillé and Mucchielli’s framework (Citation64). All stages of thematic analysis were conducted by the lead author [WJ], a doctoral student in rehabilitation sciences trained and experienced in qualitative analysis, and the study’s second author [LR], a researcher with extensive experience in qualitative methods. Although the lead author [WJ] was involved in conducting the interviews, the second author [LR] did not participate in data collection. This reduced the risk of analytical bias and ensured that the preliminary analyses did not influence the interview process. After thoroughly and repeatedly reading the transcripts, units of meaning were identified and thematized through line-by-line analysis. While the companion article focused on identifying turning points in the participants’ life trajectories, this analysis concentrated on their met and unmet needs in their daily lives and across the different services involved in their care. The themes were grouped into broader categories by identifying similarities, complementarities and differences among the data. An inductive thematic tree was constructed to structure the relationships between the categories and highlight the major themes and sub-themes. These thematic groupings were then presented to the research team for discussion and refinement, which allowed the three main themes presented in this paper to emerge.Member checking interviewsTo enhance the credibility of our findings, we sought to reestablish contact with all participants who completed the initial interviews to conduct member checking interviews (Citation65,Citation66). The recruitment process mirrored that of the initial interviews. All individuals who could be reached agreed to participate; however, several could not be contacted again due to various reasons such as disengagement from partner organizations or incarceration during the interim period. All member checking interviews were conducted by the lead author of the study [WJ]. The main themes that emerged from the thematic analysis were presented to the participants for verification of their accuracy in reflecting the participants’ actual opinions and perspectives on the issue. Participants were also encouraged to report on anything relevant to the study’s objectives that had not been identified in the analysis. These validation interviews confirmed that the results were meaningful and accurate from the participants’ point of view. In a few cases, they also provided additional insights that deepened our understanding of the significance of these themes in the participants’ lives. Incorporating this feedback further reinforced the credibility and trustworthiness of the analysis.Ethical considerationsThe research project was approved by the Research ethics committee on addiction, social inequalities and public health (project number 2024–2031). To ensure anonymity, participants were asked to choose a pseudonym that would be used to identify them throughout the research process. The names presented in this article are the pseudonyms chosen by the participants. For more information and precisions concerning ethical considerations, please refer to the companion article (Citation1).FindingsTwenty-six participants were interviewed, 16 males and 10 females. Participants ranged in age from 21 to 68 years and reported an average of 4.7 ABIs. All participants (100%) sustained a first ABI before the onset of homelessness. Using the ETHOS classification (Citation58), participants’ housing trajectories reflected a broad spectrum of homelessness and housing exclusion experiences, including living rough (category 1), staying in emergency accommodation (category 2), residing in temporary accommodation for the homeless (category 3), staying in women’s shelters (category 4), receiving long-term support due to homelessness (category 7), and living in insecure accommodation (category 8). See for the sociodemographic characteristics of the participants and for more information about the ABI-related characteristics of the sample.Table 1. Sociodemographic characteristics and general overview of sustained ABI.Three main themes emerged from the thematic analysis: 1) Intersecting health and social challenges and needs related to ABI and comorbid conditions influence residential pathways, recovery, and service use; 2) Fragmented and often inadequate service responses to complex and intersecting needs and challenges and 3) Non-use of health care services.Theme 1. Intersecting health and social challenges and needs related to ABI and comorbid conditions influence residential pathways, recovery, and service useParticipants reported various challenges present in their daily lives as a consequence of their brain injury, as well as of other mental and physical health conditions. These experiences, while not always explicitly expressed as needs, revealed significant areas where support was required. These combined challenges created needs for health, housing, and accommodation services.ABI-related needs and challenges that influence recovery and residential pathwaysSeveral participants reported the functional impacts they experienced in daily life due to the cognitive, motor, and sensory consequences of their ABI. While participants often described these impacts as symptoms or difficulties, they implicitly pointed to unmet needs for adapted support and rehabilitation. Memory loss, difficulties with sustained attention, organization, and problem solving, sensory hypersensitivity, chronic pain, fatigue, and motor and language difficulties were the consequences that emerged most strongly from participants’ interviews. Tintin, a man in his early sixties, was recovering from repeated strokes when he experienced homelessness for the first time. He reported how memory losses affected his ability to navigate shelter life:But there’s something that’s not working. I know there is. I know something isn’t working. Because sometimes I can even go up [to the locker space] four or five times when I’m going upstairs and say, what was I looking for? – Tintin.Moss, a trans woman in her early twenties, reported significant memory loss following multiple ABIs during her childhood and teenage years:I know I’ve been affected brain wise because I have no … I have no memory. I don’t even know what day it is unless someone tells me, even if I knew it earlier in the day. – Moss.Some participants also noted the affective and mental health consequences they attribute to ABI. This is the case for Kim, a woman in her mid-fifties who sustained multiple ABIs in recent years in the context of intimate partner violence:I feel like it affected me in that it made me more … depressed. Depressed, confused. Like I didn’t know what decision to make, and I was self-doubting about the decisions. And I think that came from getting hit in the head too much. – Kim.These various consequences of ABI create functional challenges in the daily lives of participants, particularly in the areas of social interactions, financial management and community navigation. Although these were described as challenges or difficulties, they reflect underlying needs for cognitive, emotional and social support. Functional limitations related to engagement in leisure and work-related activities were also noted. Social interactions were particularly challenging for participants, due to behavioral difficulties, including impulsivity, aggression, and irritability, compounded by cognitive difficulties and, for some, impaired communication skills. This was the case for Égide, a man in his early twenties, who saw radical changes in his behavior following multiple ABIs, affecting his capacity to interact with housemates:You know, before, I had trouble expressing myself. It was hell. So, you know, I was the complete opposite. I would never tell you I was angry, I would never say there was a problem. I avoided everything. And now, like, I find myself super easily in confrontation, being impulsive, and just saying whatever I’m thinking. – Égide.A similar pattern emerges for financial management, where the confluence of cognitive challenges and impulse regulation creates difficulty in planning and following a budget. Max, for example, acknowledged that his impulsivity has had a major impact on his financial management and, ultimately, his ability to maintain and obtain housing:Well, I had a problem with budgeting. I didn’t always pay my rent on time. [Interviewer: You were evicted from housing?] Yeah. [I had] trouble prioritizing. I really liked going out partying in bars and all that — I pretty much put that first, but really that should’ve come last. […] And then … a guy’s got a place for rent, and there are ten people who want it, and he sees that I’ve always had trouble paying my rent. I’m already starting with three strikes against me. – Max.Multiple and complex health and social needs and challengesThe majority of participants reported complex and multifaceted needs relating not only to their ABI, but also to other physical and mental health conditions. Many reported challenges associated with various mental health issues, including substance use disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder and mood disorders. Additionally, participants often experienced various physical health issues beyond their ABI, such as chronic pain, musculoskeletal conditions and diabetes.Several participants discussed significant needs specific to mental health issues. These needs persist despite residential stabilization, as Mr. Toujours, a man in his early fifties who recently obtained permanent housing with support explained:I knew it wouldn’t change anything [when I got permanent housing], you know. Well, in terms of my mental health, it wouldn’t change anything […] With my borderline personality disorder, I can feel sad and lonely more intensely than normal people […] I’d like to see the psychiatrist more often […] It always feels good to talk about personal things, about what’s going wrong and what’s going right. – Mr. Toujours.Max, a man in his late fifties who recently obtained a bipolar disorder diagnosis spoke about the need for close medical monitoring and management to help him function better on a daily basis:During my ‘highs’ [manic episodes], I could go four, five days without … like a guy on drugs, four, five days without sleeping […] You know, when I feel impulsive, it was during my ‘high’ moments […] If they had detected my bipolar disorder earlier, and given me medication, you know, I wouldn’t have had those moments of rage — I call it my rage — and it would have saved me a lot of problems. – Max.Many participants also discussed issues relating to emotional trauma and abuse, such as physical, psychological, or sexual assault, as well as adverse childhood experiences. These experiences, while described as psychological or behavioral challenges, also highlight the need for trauma-informed and sustained psychosocial support. Raphaël, who is in his mid-thirties, spoke about the frequent flashbacks he still experiences from childhood traumas, and the resulting behavioral consequences:It keeps coming back to me sometimes. I’m trying, but it keeps coming. Unexpectedly, it comes back to me—what happened in my past life. I almost went crazy this morning, you know? I get mad at my friends sometimes out of nowhere. – Raphaël.Several participants mentioned needs related to the use of psychoactive substances. For many, substance use is a significant challenge and is connected to many of the difficulties they have encountered. Kevin talked about his problematic substance use:I used [drugs] for a hell of a long time. Sometimes I wonder why I’m still alive today. I think back on it sometimes and say, ‘Christ! I should be dead with all the drugs I’ve taken in my life.’ It definitely doesn’t help my situation either. – Kevin.For Ali, a man in his early sixties who has struggled with substance use disorder for several years, the needs associated with his addiction pose a significant challenge to his daily life and quality of living. Although he is willing to do anything to stop, he requires assistance:I always go back to it [substance use]. I always go back to it. I always go back to it. And nothing … until I get to that point, nothing can bring joy to my life. Nothing. Nothing […] I’m weak, very weak, fragile. Everything that happens to me, I run to drugs […] I would ask the doctor to take my eyes, if that could make me quit drugs. This is how bad it is. I’m willing to go blind with no … in a wheelchair too, with no legs. Just make me quit. How? That’s the million-dollar question. – Ali.Characteristics of community and housing environments restrict participation and recoveryThe challenges and consequences associated with ABI are compounded by the characteristics of community environments, including shelters and community spaces. Such community environments are often characterized by loud noises, artificial lighting, strong smells, and proximity with other service users who may display challenging and unpredictable behaviors. Égide described how these factors contribute to his behavioral challenges:Because I have more of a concentration barrier, well, when I’m in really stimulating environments like the day center, where sometimes there’s two different kinds of music, people are talking, shouting, there’s a lot of smells, the light is bright, the more stimulating the environment, the more it interferes with my own thoughts. And then, because I’m having trouble thinking, I get kind of frustrated. – Égide.Other participants emphasized their inability to recover after being discharged from the hospital after an ABI because of the living conditions in shelters, and that they needed a calm living environment to aid their recovery. Their accounts suggest an implicit need for supported housing environments that accommodate cognitive recovery. This is the case for Catherine, a woman in her late sixties, who rapidly got discharged from the hospital following a brain surgery related to her ABI. She spoke about the difficulty of recovering in an emergency shelter:[…] They put you in a room where the girl doesn’t sleep all night, and then she sleeps during the day. And then I need to sleep, and then I have trouble sleeping. You know what I mean? […] It’s not suitable [recovery] with someone who doesn’t sleep at night, who keeps you from sleeping. – Catherine.Finally, several participants spoke about their prospects in terms of housing and accommodation, emphasizing the need for their housing to be adapted to their complex needs related to ABI and other traumatic life events. In some cases, participants expressed these as fears or safety concerns rather than direct service demands, but they nevertheless reveal a need for secure, adapted housing. For example, Minecraft99, a woman victim of intimate partner violence for several years, spoke about the need for high-security housing:I’m scared to death now. Sometimes I’m okay in a place like this [shelter]. Then, when I’m outside, I realize I’m smoking a cigarette, then there’s no one around, then, even though I’m a chronic smoker, I put out my cigarette, then I run inside. Then I ring the bell. Then sometimes I’m in the bathroom, then I’m scared. I’m scared now. I didn’t have that before. You know, when you say you’re at peace, you’re not afraid of anything. But now, I’m afraid. Even in women’s places. It’s crazy, right? – Minecraft99.What Moss really wants is a permanent home where she can isolate herself and rest and recover from her ABI:Just a roof over my head. Then I can stop talking to everybody, then I can go to bed, then I don’t go out for six months. Sleep. – Moss.Therefore, participants present complex social and health profiles, with multiple needs that require coordinated, cross-sectoral responses throughout the different services involved in their care trajectories.Theme 2. Fragmented and often inadequate service responses to complex and intersecting needs and challengesThe various services involved in caring for people experiencing homelessness with ABI, in both community and institutional settings, respond differently to the challenges and needs of the participants, whether relating to their ABI, mental health, housing situation, other medical and social conditions, or all of the above.The response of community and frontline services to complex health and ABI-related needs and difficultiesMost of the participants we met reported a positive relationship with at least one community worker or health care professional from specific teams in the health and social services network, including homelessness outreach services and frontline mental health and addiction services. Many participants described the community environment as welcoming, conducive to building trust, and able to meet a wide range of their needs. These positive connections have even enabled several participants to obtain permanent housing at some point in their lives.I have people here to help me. [They help me with] anything that has to do with family problems, whatever, if I need to take steps or whatever. Yeah, they do everything. […] It can be anything from applying for welfare to …, whatever you want. No real limits here. – Bob.Many participants said that, after several years, they had managed to build important connections with their support workers, despite a lack of trust in most people and considerable reluctance to connect with others because of the adversity they had experienced over their lifetime:Before, I didn’t talk to anyone. It was impossible for me to confide in anyone. You see, I have zero trust in the world. I have zero. I’ve had such a shitty time. So, I don’t trust anybody anymore. And then, shit, [my community workers] I’ve known them for a long time. I’ve known them for almost ten years. I’m [only now] starting to talk to them. – Kevin.However, while these community and frontline services recognize participants’ health-related needs, including the cognitive and behavioral consequences of ABI, they are neither designed nor sufficiently equipped to address these needs. This mismatch can result in key needs going unmet and lead to fragmented care, and even, exclusion from these services. Catherine, for example, talked about her perception of the lack of training for community workers:I understand that in places like this [homeless shelter], there aren’t specialized people who … well, not specialized, but who have training in care. And it’s not just brain injury. Whether it’s any kind of care, I find that the training is too technical and too regulated, which means that they have difficulty adapting to specific cases. – Catherine.Conversely, some participants have been excluded from community or frontline health services because of their challenging behaviors:After psychiatry, they put me in therapy. It was a six-month mandatory therapy, but I didn’t finish my six months. They thought I was too ‘speedy’ — not on the drug speed, but I was too hyper — so they transferred me here [to the hospital]. – Matthew.The response of specialized ABI services to social vulnerability and housing instabilitySeveral participants had access to specialized services relating to their ABI and reported being satisfied with the emergency services for ABIs, which they described as quick and efficient. For instance, many participants had access to brain scans and consultations with neurologists as part of emergency hospital consultations. Some patients with severe injuries also had access to rehabilitation services specific to their ABI. However, this initial positive experience contrasted with the lack of follow-up by the health network after this initial episode of care, despite the presence of significant persistent symptoms:[Interviewer: But you don’t think there’s any follow-up after that?] No, no, no, no, no. I was the one who called. I was the one who called. I said, ‘Hey, what are the results?’ ‘But you’re still under investigation.’ “Yes, but under investigation? I said, “What do you mean it’s not moving any further? I said, ‘If it was your son, would you move more?’ He said, ‘We’re not talking about my son, we’re talking about you.’ But I said, ‘Exactly. That’s the wrong answer. The day it’s your son, I’m sure things will move.’ – Tintin.Participants with severe injuries who were admitted to hospital-based or rehabilitation center-based ABI-specific services identified those services as poorly adapted to their social situation or mental health status. These situations resulted in early discharge and loss of follow-up from ABI-specific services, either through exclusion of services or when participants refused further involvement in care. This was the case for Buck, who returned to an emergency shelter after an early discharge from a rehabilitation center with no follow-up despite significant residual effects following a severe traumatic brain injury:I was in rehab [for my ABI] and I went outside to smoke a cigarette and it was windy. And I smoked my cigarette and all. And I don’t remember throwing it out. Anyway, to make a long story short, I went back into the place [the rehabilitation center], and I was starting a fire. The cigarette had been blown onto me, and … so I got kicked the hell out! – Buck.The (lack of) response of general health services, criminal justice services and correctional services to ABI-related needs and difficultiesMost participants reported that they did not have access to screening, assessment and referral services for their ABI in certain services, notably general health services, youth protection and criminal justice or correctional services. Some participants also spoke about the lack of training on ABI for workers in these settings and the failure to address their ABI-related needs. This is the case for The chosen one who deplored the lack of consideration for his ABI and the state of his mental health in the prison system:They should have sent me straight to [a mental health institution] to be treated by people who knew what they were doing. You can see in my file that I’m not a criminal. I’m not a drug dealer, a gangster or anything like that. Those filthy dogs in the prison system don’t understand a damn thing about rehabilitation. Rehabilitation means not turning people into criminals or killers. At [the mental health institution], they know how to treat mental health problems. They know how to talk to you and treat you. Even if they get angry with you, they’ll send you to your room, but they’ll come back and talk to you. You see, that’s what that place is for. The [prison] system? What even is that? – The chosen one.For many participants, the lack of recognition of ABI meant that they had very difficult experiences in services and received interventions that were not tailored to their needs. Some participants who had symptoms of impulsivity, hypersensitivity, and difficulty adjusting to the prison environment because of their unrecognized ABI experienced crises that were sanctioned by placements in segregation:There’s a problem in the prison system, there’s a big problem. How are they dealing with it? Look, I’ve never robbed a bank, so why are they treating me like this? A week and two days before I take a shower, sleeping on sheets that are full of shit? I was treated like … a dog is treated better than that. – The chosen one.When participants, like Égide, tried to access general health services to manage ABI-related symptoms, all their symptoms were attributed to substance use:Well, he [the family doctor] thought I was like a junkie and that I wanted drugs. Then he thought that all my symptoms could be explained by my [cannabis] use. He said I stuttered because of the cannabis. He said that I had migraines because of cannabis. He said that my diction problems were due to it […] – Égide.Therefore, although some services were described as welcoming and compassionate, participants generally reported having had difficult, even traumatic, experiences with the various services involved in their care, which, when combined with other factors such as rigid rules, sometimes resulted in them being reluctant to use these services.Theme 3. Nonuse of health care servicesSeveral participants spoke about their tendency to avoid using health services, for either urgent or non-urgent health needs, but also after a blow to the head or in the presence of symptoms related to a non-traumatic ABI. Several reasons were given by participants to explain this avoidance of services, including previous negative, non-helpful or traumatic experiences in the healthcare network:Yes, I stayed at home [when I had symptoms of stroke]. But let me tell you what they do at the hospital. They run some tests and then leave you in a fishbowl. Yes, they saw me fairly quickly every time. But still, nothing happens afterwards, you know? – Tintin.There were bars outside [the psychiatric institute]. You’d go downstairs and see fencing. It was like a real prison – a maximum-security prison, I’m telling you. It was the worst time of my life. It’s no joke – you had to keep an eye on everyone, otherwise they’d hit you or beat you up. – Poupou.However, these negative and traumatic experiences are not always solely attributed to the care and services that the participants received themselves. Rather, they are intertwined with lifelong adversity, including memories of loved ones being seriously ill or dying, and of the difficult hospital experiences surrounding these events. This makes it challenging to disentangle the painful memories from the services themselves:I have a phobia of hospitals. I have to push myself to go. I hate hospitals. […] My youngest daughter was born prematurely. She was born at 24 weeks. […] We brought her home 26 months later. I would finish work and go to the hospital. I slept at the hospital, I ate at the hospital, I basically washed myself at the hospital. We were always, always at the hospital. […] I already had issues with hospitals. When I went to the hospital, I always wanted to go with someone. I didn’t want to go alone. But now, I don’t want to go at all anymore. I want nothing to do with hospitals anymore. – Kevin.Other participants, like Ali, talked about the belief that their health would not improve or, worse, would deteriorate if they sought health care services to explain this nonuse:I don’t like hospitals […] Sometimes you’re not sick, you go to the hospital, you get sicker. I have this mentality, which is wrong, but … – Ali.Several participants also talked about the difficulty of tolerating the hospital environment because of the long waiting times involved, nonsmoking and no-use of psychoactive substances rules, the lack of access to meaningful activities, and the overwhelming sensory environment, including loud noises and bright lights:I went to the hospital, but I didn’t sign in. Too many people. Too many people. You get there, it’s full […] And you’ll see, people wait for twenty hours […] So, I don’t feel like waiting. – Tintin.I don’t want to go to the hospital. You can’t smoke, you can’t go out, you can’t do anything. – Poupou.Finally, pride in being able to cope on one’s own and not asking others for help was often cited as a reason for not using health care services, by male participants only.Look, I’m someone who never asks anything from anyone. Never, never, never, never will you see me begging anyone for anything. Never. […] Me, having a doctor for a health issue … look, I’m totally fine. I don’t ask anything from anyone […] I don’t want [help with] anything, nothing at all! – Buck.Overall, the results highlight three interrelated themes. Firstly, participants described the cognitive, emotional and social consequences of ABI, as well as other health and social challenges that shaped their daily lives and interactions with services. Secondly, they reported fragmented and often inadequate responses from the various services involved in their care, reflecting gaps in coordination and expertise. Thirdly, several participants described a pattern of disengagement or avoidance of services, which was often rooted in previous negative or traumatic experiences.DiscussionThis study identified multiple interrelated challenges, as well as met and unmet health and social needs among people experiencing homelessness and ABI in their daily lives and across various services involved in their trajectories, delivered in both community and institutional settings. The findings also revealed a fragmented and often inadequate response from the various services involved in participants’ care trajectories, as well as the importance of addressing the functional challenges that contribute to the onset and persistence of homelessness in a transactional manner that considers individual and environmental factors. The findings demonstrate that the cognitive, emotional and behavioral consequences of ABI, such as memory loss, impulsivity, fatigue and emotional dysregulation, interact with other health and social vulnerabilities, including mental health issues, trauma and substance use. When these intersecting challenges coincide with unstable housing conditions and fragmented service systems, the result is repeated episodes of service exclusion, homelessness, and disengagement from care. However, participants also described how establishing trusting relationships with community workers and having access to stable, supportive housing could promote recovery, stability, and re-engagement with services. We acknowledge that some of the findings reflect challenges or difficulties rather than explicitly stated ‘needs.’ In line with prior research on unmet needs in vulnerable populations, we considered these challenges to be indicators of areas in which services could intervene, even if participants did not express them as demands (Citation35,Citation67). This approach enabled us to capture both expressed and implicit needs within the analysis.These findings underscore the urgent need for integrated care models that bridge service silos and promote continuity, as outlined in integrated care frameworks, which call for coordinated, person-centered approaches to address complex, interrelated needs (Citation40,Citation68). Many previous studies have identified the complex and often overlapping health needs of people experiencing homelessness, regarding both physical and mental health (Citation2–6,Citation16,Citation27,Citation28). Difficult experiences in care trajectories, often resulting in unmet service needs, have also been widely reported (Citation26,Citation29–34). However, to our knowledge, this study is the first to specifically explore the needs and experiences from the perspective of individuals with lived experience of both homelessness and ABI. By highlighting the unique challenges faced by this population at the intersection of ABI-related impairments and systemic service fragmentation, this study makes a valuable contribution to the existing literature.Several specific challenges and needs identified in this study have also been documented in previous literature on ABI. For example, difficulties with financial management and challenging behaviors have been associated with housing instability and homelessness (Citation69–72). Cognitive impairments, such as short-term memory loss, poor attention, executive dysfunction and issues with impulse control, are commonly observed in individuals with an ABI, severe mental illness, or substance use disorders. These impairments can hinder the ability to manage finances, thereby increasing the risk of housing loss (Citation12,Citation69–71). These difficulties are further exacerbated by structural barriers, such as budgeting on a limited income and navigating increasingly complex financial and banking systems (Citation69). Similarly, the quality of social interactions has been previously shown to act as a powerful homelessness risk or protective factor. Challenges with social and communication skills, such as self-expression, understanding others’ expectations, problem-solving interpersonal conflicts, and asserting oneself, have been shown to impede one’s ability to find and maintain housing (Citation73). Challenging behaviors following an ABI have also been linked to various health and social issues, as well as significantly increased use of services among adults living in the community (Citation74). Conversely, characteristics of social environments such as stigmatizing attitudes or threats to safety can negatively affect one’s ability to engage in social interactions (Citation75). These findings highlight a cyclical pattern whereby a lack of access to appropriate ABI-related services results in unmet functional needs, creating barriers to accessing and maintaining proper housing. The resulting housing instability further impedes access to the services that could support recovery and community reintegration, perpetuating a cycle of exclusion.Our findings also reflect the barriers outlined in Omerov’s review (Citation37), particularly with regards to service fragmentation, the absence of adapted support for cognitive and behavioral issues, and structural obstacles that hinder long-term recovery for individuals experiencing homelessness with an ABI. The findings highlight important interpersonal barriers, such as prejudice, which can hinder service provision. However, building strong relationships with certain community or network stakeholders can positively influence individuals’ progress and recovery. In terms of structural barriers, the physical layout of residential and care environments often fails to accommodate the cognitive and behavioral challenges faced by participants. Finally, in terms of organization, our results show that service organizations struggle to deliver timely, continuous, adequately intensive services that are adapted to individuals’ long-term, complex, comorbid health and social needs (Citation76). Participants also described avoiding health services, despite having significant needs, a phenomenon that has been well documented in prior studies (Citation39,Citation77,Citation78). Our results contribute to this body of work by demonstrating that nonuse of health services occurs even when significant symptoms of ABI are present. This suggests that, despite indicating a clear need for support, these symptoms do not necessarily lead to service engagement. These findings suggest that avoidance may result not only from individual mistrust or negative experiences, but also from the cumulative impact of repeated encounters with institutional barriers. Participants who had experienced unmet expectations or exclusion from health, social and correctional systems appeared to internalize a sense of futility toward future institutional engagement, even when services were presented as supportive or beneficial.Implications for practice and policyThis study highlights the urgent need for innovative, coordinated models of care and rehabilitation service provision to address the intersecting long-term health and social needs of individuals with ABI experiencing homelessness – needs that are unmet within fragmented service systems. Recommendations from recent studies support the implementation of such models with key components including person-centered care, multidisciplinary teams, routine screening and referral for ABI within mental health and substance use services (and vice versa), cross-sector collaboration, and a sustained, long-term approach to care (Citation49,Citation79,Citation80). Routine screening for ABI within homelessness and correctional justice settings has also shown promise as a strategy to raise awareness on the ABI-related challenges and connect individuals to specialized health care (Citation81–89). Such cross-sector collaboration could be expanded beyond mental health and substance use services to include other frequently used services for people experiencing homelessness, such as infectious disease and sexual health services. Incorporating ABI-informed practices in these settings could strengthen the early detection of ABI and coordination of care for individuals with complex, multisectoral needs.Capacity building through training service providers on ABI in these settings has also shown positive outcomes (Citation55,Citation90,Citation91). Studies report improved cross-sector knowledge of ABI and correctional justice resources (Citation90), as well as enhanced self-efficacy and capacity to address the needs of individuals with ABI in homelessness settings (Citation55,Citation91). Community-based ABI rehabilitation programs represent an effective strategy to engage individuals experiencing homelessness who tend to avoid traditional healthcare services, while addressing their multiples health and social needs. Such initiatives have been implemented in a shelter-based medical respite program (Citation79), integrated primary care settings for individuals experiencing homelessness (Citation85,Citation88) and other homelessness and domestic violence settings (Citation83,Citation84) with consistently promising outcomes. Integrating functional assessments in discharge planning from correctional or health institutions, as well as during the transition into housing may contribute to better assess and meet individuals’ functional needs (Citation92,Citation93). Finally, capacity building through initial and continued training is essential for the healthcare sector to improve its understanding of, and response to, the complex health profiles and social needs of people experiencing or at risk of homelessness (Citation50,Citation94,Citation95). These implications echo the findings of a recent realist-inspired review, which showed that innovative rehabilitation models flourish when they combine clearly defined goals and long-term funding with multidisciplinary teamwork, leadership support and system-wide outreach to bridge the gaps between fragmented services (Citation96).Strengths and limitationsThis study is innovative because, to our knowledge, it is the first to specifically explore the perspectives of homeless individuals with an ABI regarding their needs and experiences in the different services involved in their care trajectories. The large and diverse sample, regarding gender, sexual orientation and migration background, is also a notable strength. An important limitation of this study is that all participants were recruited through partner community organizations, meaning that they all had contact with at least one service point. It would have been valuable to include individuals with no service contact to compare their views with those of individuals who received at least minimal support. Additionally, as community workers identified potential participants based on their subjective knowledge of clients’ life histories rather than formal ABI documentation and diagnoses, individuals with unreported or ‘invisible’ ABIs may not have been identified or invited to participate. Furthermore, community partners did not document how many clients were initially approached or declined to participate, which limits our ability to assess refusal rates and the selectivity of the sample.ConclusionThis article sheds light on the complex health and social needs of people experiencing homelessness who have sustained an ABI, and on the fragmented and often inadequate responses provided by the services involved in their care. Our findings highlight the urgent need for a more coordinated and integrated approach to care, one that is tailored to the multifaceted needs of this population and can bridge systemic gaps to support their long-term recovery and inclusion.Disclosure statementThe authors report there are no competing interests to declare.
